answer.rationale: With the line at 94% of committed volume and no buffer, any delivery disruption is unacceptable, which rules out switching to the low-cost vendor given memory_c2's documented SLA misses in three of four quarters on a critical line. The contract expires in 14 days with no auto-renew, forcing action now rather than deferral (memory_c5's deferral logic applies only to non-critical lines). memory_c4 and memory_c6 show that renegotiating at renewal and using multi-year commitments both recovered real margin/unit cost without narrowing service scope or destabilizing integration, directly serving the finance mandate to cut spend 18% while keeping TCO and delivery risk low. I verify memory_c4 to confirm the actual magnitude and terms of the prior renegotiation success, and memory_c2 to confirm the severity/frequency of the SLA failures before ruling out the low-cost alternative. Adding a second source (memory_c3) is valuable for constrained components but doesn't address the imminent contract expiration deadline this cycle, and switching entirely is too risky given zero volume buffer. Negotiating terms with the incumbent at renewal is the action that best balances the cost mandate against the delivery-risk constraint this cycle.
